questions.prompt: In a very fluid membrane, cholesterol tends to do what?

options.b: Bind sugars on the outer surface
options.c: Restrain movement of membrane components

options.b: By preventing excessive stiffening
options.c: By making the two leaflets identical

questions.prompt: According to the fluid mosaic model, membrane components can do what?

options.b: Remain fixed in one place
options.c: Switch leaflets freely

questions.prompt: Lipids rarely switch between leaflets without which help?

options.b: Glycocalyx sugars
options.c: Unsaturated double bonds

questions.prompt: Sugars on the outer surface, forming the glycocalyx, help cells do what?

options.b: Switch leaflets without enzymes
options.c: Recognize one another, including self from non-self

options.b: They differ in composition
options.c: They contain only proteins
options.d: They are separated by cholesterol layers

answer_key.rationale: Heads are water-loving, so the bilayer places them facing water on both sides.
Tails are water-avoiding, so they tuck inside the bilayer away from water.
A double bond kinks unsaturated tails, hindering close packing and increasing fluidity.
The explanation lists tail saturation, chain length, temperature, and cholesterol as fluidity factors.
In very fluid membranes, cholesterol restrains movement, buffering fluidity.
In the cold, cholesterol prevents excessive stiffening of the membrane.
The fluid mosaic model describes components that can move sideways.
Lipids rarely switch leaflets without enzymes such as flippases, floppases, and scramblases.
Glycocalyx sugars help cells recognize one another and distinguish self from non-self.
The two leaflets differ in composition, as the explanation states.

payload.explanation_text: A cell membrane is a flexible boundary. Phospholipids have water-loving heads and water-avoiding tails: this combination is called amphipathic. They form a bilayer with heads toward water on both sides and tails tucked inside. Saturated fatty acid tails pack closely. Double bonds kink unsaturated tails, making close packing harder and increasing fluidity. Fluidity describes how freely membrane components move. Tail saturation, chain length, temperature, and cholesterol affect it. Cholesterol buffers fluidity: it restrains movement when the membrane is very fluid and prevents excessive stiffening in the cold. The fluid mosaic model describes a mixture of lipids, cholesterol, and proteins whose components can move sideways. The two membrane layers, or leaflets, differ in composition. Lipids rarely switch leaflets without enzymes such as flippases, floppases, and scramblases. Sugars on the outer surface form the glycocalyx and help cells recognize one another, including distinguishing self from non-self.

concepts.name: Membrane asymmetry and lipid flipping
